title: North West cancels music tour days before first show
summary: North West has canceled what would have been her first headlining tour, just months after launching her music career and only days before the first show.
story: North West has canceled what would have been her first headlining tour, just months after launching her music career and only days before the first show.
The 13-year-old daughter of Kim Kardashian and Kanye West released her debut EP, “N0rth4evr,” in May and was set to hit the road next week with rapper Molly Santana, 21, on the Kimokawaii Tour.
But on Thursday, West announced the tour would no longer move forward.
“I was really excited to go on tour w Molly Santana,” she wrote on her Instagram story, according to E! News. “Sadly it isn’t happening anymore.”
The teen did not explain why the tour was cancelled, but hinted at another project, adding alongside a black heart emoji, “But I have something special for u guys see ya soon.”

The tour was scheduled to begin August 5. in Dallas and run through Aug. 27, ending in Los Angeles. All 14 tour dates listed are now marked as canceled on Ticketmaster, and the tour’s official website has been taken down.
West’s debut EP was released in May, with several members of the Kardashian-Jenner family promoting her music on social media.

“To everyone who bought tickets to the tour, I sincerely apologize,” Santana wrote Thursday on her Instagram story. “Nothing makes me more happy than the opportunity to share more amazing memories with you all, and I hope to see you soon.”

title: Letters sent to Nancy Guthrie’s family after her disappearance are released
summary: Two ransom notes purportedly sent by those who kidnapped Nancy Guthrie in Arizona earlier this year were released Friday by local authorities hoping to generate new leads in the case.
story: Two ransom notes purportedly sent by those who kidnapped Nancy Guthrie in Arizona earlier this year were released Friday by local authorities hoping to generate new leads in the case.
The second note, sent Feb. 6 to a Tucson news outlet, states that Guthrie, 84, died shortly after she was taken.

“We believe it was heart related,” the note says. “She is buried in nature now. Nothing you could have done could have changed the outcome. We want your family to know this and hope you all can find peace. We are truly sorry.”
The 84-year-old mother of “TODAY” co-host Savannah Guthrie went missing from her home near Tucson early Feb. 1. The FBI has said her disappearance is being investigated as a kidnapping for ransom.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
The first note, sent on Feb. 2 to the same outlet, a CBS affiliate, stated that a white smartwatch was on the floor at the foot of her bed and that the flood light in the backyard had been destroyed.
That note demanded a payment of $4 million in bitcoin by Feb. 5.

It provided a deadline of 5 p.m. Feb. 9 and raised the ransom amount to $6 million if the payment was not immediately made. The note warned that Nancy Guthrie was aware that “her life is in your hands.”
“Do not play games, law enforcement will not be able to help you,” the note states.
In a news release accompanying the notes, the Pima County Sheriff’s Department said Friday it was releasing the letters in an effort to generate new leads.

The notes reveal a “unique linguistic style” with distinctive word choice, syntax and phraseology, the department said, and provide “valuable insight into the person’s mindset, motives, and the evolution of their tone over time.”

“The distinctive linguistic characteristics may be recognizable to someone who knows or has interacted with the notes’ writer,” the release says. “A friend, family member, coworker, classmate or acquaintance may recognize these patterns of expression and possess information that could help identify the individual responsible.”
Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos told NBC News on Friday that the notes were released in an effort to reach whoever knows the person or persons responsible.
“All the investigators agree: There is somebody out there that knows something. They know who did this,” Nanos said.

“We want to hear from those who know who did this,” he said. “It could be a family member, it could be a brother, a sister, a friend, a neighbor. We just want to hear from you. And I think the notes speak for themselves.”
The release underscores the state of the investigation. Authorities do not have any suspects or leads of significance, so they’re requesting the public’s help.
Such a release is not without precedent. For years, the FBI struggled with releasing the writings of an unnamed suspect who became known as “Unabomber.”

That suspect had asked for his writings to be published. Following the publication of his screed, family members of the suspect now known to be Ted Kaczyinski, alerted the FBI through an attorney after examining other writings from Kaczyinski sent to the family over the years.

That lead, which was one of 50,000 the FBI received over the course of that case, ultimately led to Kaczyinski’s shed in the mountains of Montana. He was also the 2,416th person to be examined by the FBI in the case.
In the Guthrie case, authorities redacted a line that references how to get payment to the person or persons who sent the note, officials said.
There is a law enforcement reason for that redaction, according to the officials.

Former FBI supervisory special agent Jason Pack said that while there isn’t enough text in the notes to guess the author’s age or schooling, they appear to have been written by a native English speaker who uses an idiom and small connecting words appropriately at a length that’s hard to fake.
Savannah Guthrie shares new plea to bring her mother home

“And he writes like someone who spends his day sending business email,” Pack said. “‘Money in the amount of. Payment that will need to be paid by. Wanting to have this completed.’ That is office language, and it sits strangely against the threats, which sound like they came off a television screen.”
“If you knew this man, that is the part you would recognize,” Pack said. “Not his vocabulary. His habits.”
The notes’ release came days after Savannah Guthrie made an emotional plea online to the person who may have taken her mother, urging them to “do the right thing” and “tell us where to look for her.”
“I’m coming on today with a very specific message,” Savannah  Guthrie said in a video posted on social media.

“It has been months since our mom was taken from us. Our family is in agony. We are in a nightmare that will not end. Nothing about our situation has changed. We have done our part, and we will never stop looking for her. We will always ache for her and feel that hole in our hearts.”

“The world can be a cruel and unforgiving place, and I know that you have tried to do things the right way,” she said. “So I am asking you — begging you — to do the right thing now. Make the right choice. Help us find her. Tell us where to look for her. I truly believe it is never too late to do the right thing. Help us bring this situation to an end.”
Anyone with information is urged to contact 1-800-CALL-FBI (1-800-225-5324). The Guthrie family is also offering a $1 million reward for the return of her mother.

title: Decorated Army vet files $3M claim alleging National Guard assault
summary: National Guard members shoved a retired Army captain to the pavement in violent retaliation for her opposition to their deployment in Washington, D.C., the decorated soldier said in a multimillion-dollar administrative claim filed this week.
story: National Guard members shoved a retired Army captain to the pavement in violent retaliation for her opposition to their deployment in Washington, D.C., the decorated soldier said in a multimillion-dollar administrative claim filed this week.
The confrontation unfolded May 8 in front of the home of retired Capt. Anna King, on New York Avenue NW in the district, she said in her claim filed against the Defense Department on Tuesday.

King, 44, was sitting on a bench outside her home at about 7:05 p.m. when “three National Guardsmen walked through the gate and announced they were” apprehending her, though they “did not have a warrant and did not explain the basis for” detaining her, according to the complaint made against the Idaho National Guard.

The guard members “grabbed her arms and back and shoved her toward the concrete patio” before two of them “pressed their weight down on her and cuffed her wrists behind her back, extraordinarily tightly, with plastic handcuffs,” King’s legal team wrote.

“Ms. King repeatedly screamed in pain, but the Guardsmen continued to hold her down and did nothing to help her. One Guardsmen pressed his knee into her back and pulled her arms upward, increasing the pain,” according to the injury claim seeking $3 million.

“A Guardsman squatted on top of Ms. King, holding onto the handcuffs, for about eight minutes, keeping her immobilized, her face against the concrete. As additional National Guardsmen arrived on scene, Ms. King complained that her shoulder hurt and pleaded for the Guard members to loosen the handcuffs, but no one did. She asked why she was being detained but received no response.”
A Metropolitan Police Department officer allegedly told King’s neighbor that night that the former Army captain was a suspect in an assault on a guard member days earlier.
That allegation is “baseless” and no such charges have ever been filed against King, her legal team said.
King, in her claim, said she’d been a vocal critic of the National Guard patrolling Washington, D.C.
King said she had displayed signs at her home, including “Occupation: Troops Out” and “National Guard Stop Being So Embarrassing,” according to the complaint.
The “only apparent reason the Guards targeted Ms. King was her speech, via the prominent signs in her window, criticizing their presence in the District,” according to the claim.
A Defense Department official declined to comment on King’s allegations on Friday.
“As a matter of longstanding policy, the Department does not comment on ongoing litigation,” the representative said.
The Trump administration said it deployed the National Guard to various U.S. cities — such as Los Angeles, Chicago, Portland, Oregon, and Washington, D.C. — in an effort to battle crime.
The Defense Department said earlier this month that the National Guard will remain deployed in Washington, D.C., through Inauguration Day in 2029.
King served in Iraq and has received a Bronze Star and a Purple Heart for her service, according to her claim.

title: Judge denies request by Elon Musk’s xAI to pause Minnesota nudification ban
summary: A judge denied a request from Elon Musk’s AI company xAI to block Minnesota’s law that will be the first in the nation to ban nudification technology.
story: A federal judge on Friday denied a request from Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company xAI to block a Minnesota law that will be the first in the nation to ban nudification technology.

U.S. District Judge Donovan Frank ruled that there was little risk of immediate harm from the law going into effect as scheduled on Saturday, despite a lawsuit this week from xAI claiming that the law violates the First Amendment’s guarantee of free speech.

“xAI filed the motion on July 29, 2026, nearly three months after the law was signed, and only three days before the law is set to take effect. Such a delay in bringing the action and the motion suggests that harm is not immediate,” the judge wrote in a two-page order, denying xAI’s request for a pause to the law.
The court could still pause the law at a later time. The judge wrote that he’ll hold a hearing on Aug. 19 on whether to grant a preliminary injunction.

The law, which was signed by Democratic Gov. Tim Walz in May, prohibits a person who owns or controls a website, application or software to allow their users to “nudify” images of others. It also prohibits anyone from advertising nudification capabilities.

In its lawsuit filed Monday, Musk’s company did not dispute Minnesota’s interest in banning nudification websites and apps, but said: “The law is overinclusive and there are far less restrictive alternatives that function to achieve the same ends.”

Grok, one of xAI’s products, has faced severe scrutiny for its “Imagine” feature, which uses AI to generate and edit images and videos of users. After the release of a December model, Grok began producing sexualized deepfakes of people with less clothing at the request of users on a massive scale, prompting worldwide outcry and investigations in several jurisdictions. In January, Apple threatened to remove Grok from its app store unless it made changes.
As recently as April, Grok was continuing to generate sexualized images of people without their consent, as users tried to break through restrictions that xAI put in place in January.

Minnesota’s law defines a “nudified” image or video as something that has been “altered or generated to depict an intimate part not depicted in an original unaltered image or video of an identifiable individual.”
The law applies only when “the altered or generated image or video is so realistic that a reasonable person would believe that the intimate part belongs to the identifiable individual.”
In response to the lawsuit, Walz posted on X Tuesday, “See you in court, creep.”

Violating Minnesota’s law could result in a civil penalty of up to $500,000 “for each unlawful access, download or use,” in addition to civil penalties for mental anguish, punitive damages, attorney’s fees or “other relief the court deems just and equitable.” The law says the state’s attorney general may enforce it and that victims may sue on their own. The law does not include criminal penalties.

Keith Ellison, the attorney general of Minnesota, filed a response to xAI’s lawsuit on Friday, urging the court to deny xAI’s request for a temporary restraining order, to convert it into a preliminary injunction motion, and proceed from there. Ellison argued that xAI waited too long — three months after the law was passed — to file an emergency delay, and that its “voluntary delay should not create a manufactured emergency for the Attorney General or the Court.”

xAI’s criticism of the law is drawing support from some free-speech advocates including the American Civil Liberties Union of Minnesota, which supported passage of the law in an earlier form in February but has since turned against it.

“While we believe that creating the technology to alter or ‘nudify’ photos of identifiable people is protected by the First Amendment, we also recognize that the non-consensual creation and dissemination of such material can inflict damage on people appearing in those images,” the ACLU of Minnesota said in a statement Friday.

“In engaging with lawmakers on this issue, we hoped to strike an appropriate balance between First Amendment rights and the ability of people harmed to seek remedial measures, not unlike the remedies available to people harmed by defamation. The final version of the bill does not strike that balance,” the organization said.
xAI argued that it already prohibits users “from generating nude or sexualized images of people without their consent.”

SpaceX, xAI’s parent company, faces class action lawsuits from plaintiffs who claim Grok’s AI chatbot created or shared nude deepfakes of them as children or as adults. The lawsuits also say that xAI failed to alert authorities to the alleged perpetrators who used the tool to create their nude deepfakes.

Minnesota’s law was passed amid wider efforts to regulate AI platforms that can generate deepfakes. In July, San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu sent Apple and Google cease-and-desist letters demanding they remove nudification apps from their app stores.

xAI’s lawsuit argued that creating images and videos using Grok Imagine is a protected First Amendment activity, and that Minnesota’s law did not provide a “safe harbor for good-faith efforts” by companies to avoid nudification efforts.

“Liability attaches even if the depicted persons consented — or created the image themselves — and even if the image is never shared,” xAI’s lawsuit said. “Liability also attaches even if the image has artistic, scientific, political, satirical, educational, medical, or religious value, and (again) even if the company has deployed near-perfect, state-of the-art technical controls to prevent the generation of nude images.”

The lawsuit included several examples of screenshots that it said would be banned under Minnesota’s law including one image shared by President Donald Trump showing him and other lawmakers floating shirtless in the Reflecting Pool at the National Mall.
The Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression, a free speech group, said it agreed that the state law is overly broad.

“Minnesota’s law is supposed to stop AI-generated nude images, but it’s written so broadly that it could end up covering benign political memes too, like President Trump in a bikini or former President Obama in hotpants,” John Coleman, legislative council for AI and free expression at the foundation, said in a statement. “That goes far beyond prohibiting unlawful content like child sexual abuse material, which is already illegal. Instead, it sweeps in ordinary political speech and satire that Americans create and share online every day.”
“Americans have a First Amendment right to joke about, criticize, and parody public figures. A law that reaches that expression deserves to be struck down by the courts,” Coleman said.

title: Vermont’s GOP governor defends state-run elections and mail-in voting
summary: Vermont’s GOP governor, Phil Scott, defended mail-in voting and state-run elections as a good option for Americans, rejecting Trump’s calls for the Republicans to “nationalize” elections and limit options for mail-in voting.
story: Vermont’s GOP Gov. Phil Scott on Friday defended mail ballots and state-run elections, rejecting President Donald Trump’s calls for Republicans to “nationalize” elections and limit options for mail-in voting.

Asked how he responds to Trump’s call for voting to be nationalized, Scott said he goes back to the 10th Amendment, noting that it’s “clear on the role of the states in terms of elections. So I think that we should follow that and we’re closer to the people.”

“In Vermont, I would have to say, mail-in ballots are popular. Who are they popular with? Republicans,” Scott told “Meet the Press” moderator Kristen Welker during a common ground conversation with North Carolina Democratic Gov. Josh Stein at the National Governors Association meeting in Oklahoma City.
The governor added that mail-in voting has increased voter participation among members of his party in his state, which in turn has boosted GOP representation in the state Legislature.
“We’re closer to our people and we know what’s right and what’s wrong, and we can control the elections,” Scott added, defending the role of states in administering elections.

“I would hope that all, if not the majority, of Democrats would agree that this is ours, not the federal government’s,” he said. “We were here before the federal government was, the states were, and so we formed the government. Now they’re getting bloated, and we need to protect our rights.”
Scott’s remarks come as Trump this year has continued his yearslong opposition to mail-in voting, falsely claiming that it is rife with fraud and abuse.
The claims have fueled the president’s desire to pass the SAVE America Act, a major piece of federal legislation to overhaul election administration, that has stalled in Congress.

Trump has repeatedly said that the bill would ban mail-in voting in most cases, which is not true, though the SAVE Act would impose additional requirements for citizens before registering to vote and casting a ballot.
The president himself, in a Florida special election earlier this year, voted by mail, saying it was alright for him to do so because “I’m president of the United States.”
Still, he continued to call mail-in voting “mail-in cheating” after using that method to vote.
Earlier this year, Trump also said in a podcast interview that Republicans should aim to “nationalize the voting,” comments that drew condemnation from both sides of the aisle.

White House spokeswoman Abigail Jackson on Friday responded to Scott’s remarks by saying in a statement that Trump “is committed to ensuring that Americans have full confidence in the administration of elections.” She said the president “will also continue urging Congress to pass the SAVE America Act.”

In federal courts, the Trump administration has defended an executive order the president signed that aimed to create federal lists of voters and would have required mail-in ballots to be sent only to voters on those lists. A federal judge last month blocked that order, saying it’s unconstitutional for the federal government to intervene in the administration of state elections. Trump has appealed the case to the Supreme Court, asking for permission to impose the executive order as soon as August so that it can be in effect for the upcoming midterm elections.

Scott’s comments Friday came during a moderated conversation with Stein, who said Trump’s repeated disparagement of mail-in voting and the current election system “is immensely damaging to the health of our democracy.”

The pair also spoke about a lawsuit that Vermont and North Carolina have signed onto opposing the Trump administration’s decision to condition the release of some state funds for emergency preparedness on compliance with the president’s demands for election administration reforms.

“When a disaster strikes, our objective, whether it’s local government, state government or federal government, must be to do everything in our power to save life and to help people get their lives back together,” Stein said. “So the notion that you would condition that on a state agreeing to something is offensive.”

Still, Stein said, some of the proposed reforms to the Federal Emergency Management Agency would be a “step in the right direction,” in making a process for disaster response that’s led by states and assisted by the federal government.

“When you think about something like a disaster, it should be locally driven, state managed and federally supported. And so, the resources are where it’s really critical that the federal government step up,” the North Carolina governor said.

He added later, “There’s the FEMA Review Council, and initially they were talking about eliminating FEMA altogether, and I was opposed to that. And now what they’re heading toward is much more flexibility and quicker money to states, so that we can then respond quickly, and that’s a step in the right direction.”

The two governors also spoke about the Trump administration’s mass deportation agenda and called for lawmakers in Congress to pass lasting immigration reform, which Stein and Scott each said would take rising above the current political rhetoric.

“We need more immigration from my standpoint. Legal immigration. There’s got to be a pathway to do that,” Scott said, adding that it could happen if lawmakers forget about “partisanship, elections, thinking about who’s going to be in power, what can we do to leverage this to get in power.”
He added, “Forget about the next election. Just do the right thing, and nine times out of 10, that’s what works.”
Stein agreed, telling Welker, “Our immigration system does not work well. Congress refuses to act. They are too happy to score political points rather than to address a real problem.”

title: Trump defends ‘anti-weaponization’ fund, further complicating Blanche nomination
summary: Republicans Thom Tillis and John Cornyn have been holding up Todd Blanche’s nomination for attorney general, seeking assurances the controversial fund is dead.
story: WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Friday defended his administration’s controversial proposal for a $1.8 billion “anti-weaponization fund” for Jan. 6 defendants and others who he says were unfairly targeted by the government.

Trump’s continued flirtation with the weaponization fund undermines assurances from his acting Attorney General Todd Blanche and others in the administration that the idea, which faces strong opposition from some key Republicans, is dead.
The issue delayed for several weeks and nearly derailed a $70 billion bill to fund Immigration and Customs Enforcement and the Border Patrol through the end of Trump’s term.

And it has thrown Blanche’s nomination to be the nation’s chief law enforcement official into limbo, with two Republicans — Sens. John Cornyn of Texas and Thom Tillis of North Carolina — blocking it over concerns about the settlement between Trump and the IRS that created the weaponization fund.
Add NBC News to Google
Add NBC News to Google
But Trump’s comments Friday are only worsening tensions with the two senators.

Asked Friday at a Cabinet meeting whether the fund is dead, Trump replied: “It is dead, but you know, I wish it weren’t. To be honest with you, I think people were horribly treated, horribly abused. This has nothing to do with Todd.”
Blanche is now unlikely to be confirmed before the Senate departs next week for its five-week summer recess. The chamber is not slated to return until after Labor Day.

In a post on Truth Social earlier in the day, Trump specifically lashed out at Cornyn, suggesting that the longtime senator was standing in the way of the Blanche nomination because the president had backed a primary challenger, Ken Paxton, who defeated Cornyn in May.

“John Cornyn never had a problem with the so called ‘Fund,’ which will not benefit me, but rather the great American Patriots who were hunted down like dogs and whose lives were unfairly and illegally destroyed by the Crooked Joe Biden Administration, until after I decided to Endorse and Support his Republican Primary opponent in Texas, who easily won the Nomination for the United States Senate,” Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that Cornyn had been among the Republicans who had decried the FBI’s 2022 raid on Mar-a-Lago.
“I will always feel that these victims of government abuse should be paid back for what they were forced to endure, their lives have been ruined!” he wrote.
“Todd Blanche, a good man, should be immediately approved as U.S. Attorney General,” Trump added.

Cornyn has not directly responded to Trump’s post. But on Friday, he retweeted two individuals who questioned Trump’s comments on X. One was GOP strategist Steven Duffield, who wrote: “This does not sound like citizen Trump has agreed to end the Fund.”

Responding to Trump’s post, Tillis on Friday wrote on social media, “The President made it clear today that the so-called Anti Weaponization Fund is still alive, which is exactly why we are attempting to formally end it.”
Blanche, Tillis said, “has been forthright, thoughtful and patient.”
The senator added that Blanche’s confirmation has “hit a snag only because an incompetent personal advisor to the President refuses to amend the bogus settlement.”
“Anyone who attacked law enforcement should still be in prison, not getting a check from the federal government,” Tillis said.
During his Senate confirmation hearing this month, Blanche testified that the Trump administration was abandoning plans for the weaponization fund and that it was “dead.”
But the administration has yet to put anything in writing stating it will not try to launch the fund in the future — something that has raised alarm bells with some skeptics like Cornyn.
“What it suggests to me is they are looking for an out to do something different than what Todd Blanche testified to at his hearing,” Cornyn told reporters Thursday, “and that’s a problem.”
Both Cornyn and Tillis serve on the powerful Senate Judiciary Committee. And a single GOP defection means that Blanche’s nomination cannot get out of committee and be sent to the full Senate.

Judiciary Chairman Chuck Grassley, R-Iowa, was forced to punt a Thursday vote to advance Blanche’s nomination until outstanding issues could be resolved. Grassley said he was committed to finding a resolution on Blanche.
“I’m not going to consider any other options because there’s no reason to consider other options at this point,” the chairman told reporters Thursday.

The Senate Judiciary Committee on Friday night scheduled a vote for Tuesday morning on Blanche’s nomination, despite no announced changes from Cornyn or Tillis. A spokesperson for the committee said in a statement that scheduling the meeting now “gives more time for the White House to secure the votes for the President’s nominee.”

Both Tillis and Cornyn huddled with Blanche Thursday afternoon for about 45 minutes, according to a source familiar with the meeting. The three worked in a positive, collaborative manner in an attempt to resolve the IRS settlement issues, the source added.

There’s another issue with the IRS settlement that could cause problems for Blanche: It includes an agreement that the IRS will not prosecute Trump, his family members or his businesses over any tax claims through May of this year. Both Tillis and Cornyn have said that deal should be narrowed.

Also on Friday, Trump, his sons Don Jr. and Eric and the Trump Organization on Friday filed notice they were appealing the judge’s order that found their IRS lawsuit (which led to the settlement) was brought in “bad faith” and for an “improper purpose.” U.S. District Judge Kathleen Williams found earlier this month that the facts of the case show it was “an attempt to use the Court to provide some legitimacy to an agreement to confer immunity to people and entities affiliated with the President,” while spending billions of taxpayer dollars.
Blanche’s challenges may not be confined to just Cornyn and Tillis, who is not seeking re-election this fall. “We’re just on the front line because we’re in the Judiciary,” Cornyn said.

Indeed, Sen. Bill Cassidy, R-La., whom Trump also worked to successfully defeat in a GOP primary this year, also expressed concerns about Blanche’s nomination, telling reporters, “I am very concerned about the weaponization of the Justice Department.”
“Shouldn’t every American be afraid of the weaponization of the Justice Department? If there’s not adequate answers for that, then probably there needs to be somebody else,” Cassidy said of Blanche.

title: Immigrant who donated lifesaving kidney to his brother is detained by ICE again
summary: José Gregorio González, who’s been his brother’s caregiver since the kidney transplant, was detained during a routine ICE check-in.
story: José Gregorio González is inside an immigration detention center almost a year after he donated his kidney to save the life of his brother, who has end-stage renal disease.
The Venezuelan man was taken into ICE custody July 21 during a routine check-in appointment with immigration authorities in Chicago.

González had been reporting to Immigration and Customs Enforcement since April on a weekly basis, sometimes more than once. The agency had placed him in an intensive supervision program to monitor his whereabouts after his yearlong humanitarian parole expired, according to his lawyer and brother.
“I don’t really see a need to necessarily detain him,” said Peter Meinecke, an attorney handling his immigration case and the managing attorney at Resurrection Project, a nonprofit group in Chicago.
“He has no criminal record and has been dutifully complying with supervision,” Meinecke told NBC News.

José Alfredo Pacheco, González’s younger brother and the recipient of his kidney, had just finished a follow-up medical appointment to monitor his recovery from the transplant he received last August. He texted González to let him know he was on his way to pick him up from his ICE check-in.
“Three minutes later, he replied, ‘Brother, I love you. They’re about to deport me.’ That was the only thing he wrote to me,” Pacheco told Noticias Telemundo in Spanish on Wednesday.
“My world came crashing down,” he said, noting that González is his sole caregiver. “My biggest fear is being left alone here.”

González’s story first made headlines in March 2025, when ICE detained him before he could donate his kidney to Pacheco. Community members in the Chicago area rallied in support of the brothers and advocated for González’s release under humanitarian parole. The brothers share the same mother.
González was temporarily released from ICE detention that April, and the brothers successfully underwent a lifesaving kidney transplant surgery in August.

“Someone who’s committed a very selfless act, like donating a kidney, is still being treated like they’re a threat to this country,” Meinecke said. “It’s an alarming precedent to be setting in terms of how we’re treating immigrants in this country.”
According to the Department of Homeland Security, González first attempted to enter the U.S. in June 2023, but Border Patrol arrested him and removed him from the country.

In December 2023, Pacheco was diagnosed with end-stage renal disease. González returned to the U.S. a month later, in January 2024, to care for his brother, who at the time needed four-hour dialysis sessions three times a week.
“In violation of our nation’s laws, he illegally re-entered the country,” a DHS spokesperson said about González’s January 2024 entry into the U.S.

González sought asylum but did not pass an initial credible fear interview, so immigration authorities placed a deportation order on him. Still, he was allowed to remain in the country under ICE supervision and with an ankle monitor to track him, which is not uncommon.
Before González’s humanitarian parole was set to expire in April, Meinecke said he filed a request to temporarily stop the government from enforcing the deportation order against his client.
That application was still pending when ICE detained González last week, Meinecke said.
According to the DHS spokesperson, González overstayed his parole in “violation of our nation’s laws.”
Meinecke said they intend to try to request another humanitarian parole for release from detention.
“While his health has more or less progressed the way you would hope following a surgery,” the attorney said about González, “his brother’s hasn’t been as straightforward.”

Pacheco said he has had two setbacks on the delicate journey to recovery from his kidney transplant. The worse one, a severe blood infection, landed him in the hospital in January. When he felt like he almost didn’t make it, Pacheco said his brother “was the only one who was with me.”

As a living organ donor, González is also under structured medical supervision to ensure his remaining kidney adapts well, Pacheco said. “He still has to attend his medical appointments, and there is no health care in Venezuela,” he said.

Venezuela’s fragile health care system had been deteriorating for years before two powerful earthquakes rattled the South American nation last month, killing more than 5,000 people and further exacerbating its ongoing health crisis.
The DHS spokesperson said González will “remain in ICE custody pending removal proceedings” to Venezuela.

On Sunday, Pacheco spoke to González, who called him from an immigration detention center in Missouri, where he is being held. Pacheco said his older brother never complained about the situation and instead insisted he not worry about him.
“It’s very hard when we siblings are so close,” Pacheco said with emotion. “We would give our lives for one another. … He is the best of us all.”

title: The internet is obsessed with Jellycats, but are they worth the splurge? We tested them to find out
summary: Jellycat plushies are all over TikTok, but are they worth $25 to $100 a pop? NBC Selected editors share their honest, firsthand take on the popular toy brand.
story: If you’ve spent any time on TikTok or wandered past a display of impossibly soft stuffed animals at a gift shop, you’ve probably met a Jellycat. The British brand has become one of the most collected (and gifted) soft toy lines around, with fans anticipating new “drops” the same way sneakerheads camp out for limited releases.

With the classic Bashful Bunny, the ever-expanding Amuseables food and object collection, and characters like a plush turtle that’s considerably grumpy, Jellycat has built a cult following among babies, teens and adults alike. Even scoring a reservation at the brand’s Jellycat Diner inside New York City’s iconic toy store FAO Schwartz rivals some of the best restaurants in Manhattan (rather than actual food, you’ll see adorable culinary-themed plushies on the menu).

But with prices that can range from $25 for a small Amuseable to $70 for the diner experience and over $100 for bigger stuffies, is a Jellycat actually worth it, or are you just paying for the name? To find out, I turned to other NBC Selected editors who are well versed in the Jellycat world.

Our honest review of Jellycat

The below list includes Jellycats that NBC Selected staffers personally own or have given loved ones as gifts. They also showcase the range of options available from the brand, including collectable toys and ones made for smaller children.
Jellycat Bashful Bunny

Jellycat’s Bashful Bunny is the toy that built the brand’s reputation, and it’s easy to see why. The fur is dense but not stiff and the actual bunny is stuffed enough that it feels plush to hug (but not so much that it feels too firm to cuddle with). It comes in more than a dozen colors, including the original beige, blush, lilac and cream, plus seasonal variations that show up and sell out fast.

My mom bought my daughter a now-sold-out version of this bunny with floral fabric sewn into its ears when she was first born. Five years later, the bunny is still one of her favorite stuffies. I’ve washed it a number of times and it still looks great; it looks well-loved, but still holding its shape. The floppy limbs and beanbag-weighted bottom also make it comfortable to hold or prop up.

If Bashful is Jellycat’s flagship line, Fuddlewuddle is its quieter, arguably more practical sibling. This elephant (and its many animal counterparts, like lions and dragons) has a slightly shorter, smoother fur than Bashful, which is easier to clean and less prone to matting.

The Fuddlewuddle line is also noticeably lighter, which makes it nice for a younger cuddler. While my daughter loves her bunny, she tends to sleep with this elephant more often because it feels lighter in her arms and cozier to snuggle up with.

I bought the Zumblebi Alien for my son’s space-themed bedroom, and it fits right in. One of the fun things about Jellycats is that the brand provides backstories for many of their characters. For example, this little guy has apparently seen galaxies few of us can imagine, yet he crash-landed near London Bridge decades ago and never really left. He’s since become, in Jellycat’s telling, the universe’s most devoted postcard collector, with walls covered in his cosmic collage of earthly souvenirs. It’s a charming bit of backstory that makes him feel like more than just a stuffed toy and rather a character with his own quirky little life.
In real life, my son loves to hug him because he’s extra fuzzy and bright; there’s something about that soft, saturated color and dense plush texture that makes him irresistible to squeeze.

The Amuseables line is where Jellycat’s sense of humor really shows up, and these marshmallows are a great example. The pink and white sweet treats have equally saccharine smiles and have little brown boots for flair. The duo is connected by a small ribbon so you never lose one.

NBC Selected updates editor Mili Godio, who has been a huge fan of the brand for years, has these marshmallows (as well as the Amuseables Jellysaucer). She loves the silly nature of the Amuseables line: “They’re so adorable and add so much joy; every new Jellycat addition to my desk or home is like a breath of fresh air,” she says. “I love that there’s so many unique and niche options to choose from. I currently have my eye on the Monstera plant, boiled egg and pair of olives.”

Jellycat’s bag charms, which are miniature versions of characters like Peanut, Fergus Frog and various fruits, have become a low-cost entry point for adult collectors who want in on the trend without committing to a full-size plush. At under $30, they’re some of the most affordable items in the lineup, and the clip attachment is sturdy enough to survive being tossed around.

They make especially good gifts for loved ones. “While Jellycats are pretty pricey, I find the keychains to be a good entry point,” says NBC Selected contributor Marilyn La Jeunesse. “I like that they can come along with you on all your adventures. Plus, I love knowing that if I travel to London, Paris, Seoul, or Shanghai, I can stop by and pick up an exclusive style sold only in that city. It’s like a worldwide treasure hunt.” For those not in the know, there are exclusive Jellycats available in different countries and at different retailers. For example, you can find a maple leaf Jellycat in Canada and a British tea bag in the United Kingdom.

The Bartholomew Bear Pouch takes Jellycat’s most beloved teddy bear and reimagines him as a soft, huggable little accessory you can carry everywhere. You can use it to stash small essentials like your lip balm and hand lotion, or to organize your chargers while traveling. The pouch is relatively small and just big enough to fit an iPhone, wallet and a few other small items.

Candidly, I tend to lean practical over cutesy when it comes to my accessories, but I grabbed this pouch for myself when shopping for stuffies with my daughter and love it. It stands out in my tote, so I never have to dig deep to grab it,  and it adds a moment of joy to my day anytime I pull it out. It’s also a great conversation starter; I’ve had so many strangers stop and compliment it.
What can improve
While we’ve loved collecting and testing our own Jellycats, there are few things to be aware of:

Inventory is unpredictable. Popular colors and characters sell out quickly and are sometimes retired for good, which drives up resale prices on secondhand marketplaces and can be frustrating if you’re chasing a specific item. For example, I’ve had my eye on the Amuseables Mozzarella, but it sold out quickly and has not been restocked. The Jellycat site does have a Back in Stock page that you can check to see if any of your favorites are available again.Pricing climbs fast with size. Many Jellycats come in different sizes and the jump from a small plush pal to a “huge” or “really big” version can mean paying triple or more for a toy that isn’t necessarily triple the quality — you’re simply paying for scale.Not all lines are equally durable. While Bashful and Fuddlewuddle held up well to washing, a few of the more delicate Amuseables with suedette or felt details can show early signs of wear with heavy handling, according to some of our editors.

For example, I’ve had my eye on the Amuseables Mozzarella, but it sold out quickly and has not been restocked. The Jellycat site does have a Back in Stock page that you can check to see if any of your favorites are available again.
